title: Who drew Africa's borders?
subtitle: The Scramble for Africa
subject: histoire
description: On the map, Africa's borders look as if they were drawn with a ruler. They were actually born of treaties, local wars and a choice made by the independent states, not of a single meeting in Berlin.
author: vedran-obucina

hero.hook: The straight lines on the map of Africa were not drawn with a ruler in one evening in Berlin.

blocks.text: On a map of Africa, many borders run in straight lines, as if drawn with a ruler. It is tempting to imagine a single hand behind the design. Yet no one person and no one meeting carved up the whole continent. Most of today's borders date from the rapid spread of European colonial power in the **19th century**.

The best-known starting point is the [[Berlin Conference]] of **1884-1885**. There, the European powers set the rules for acquiring colonies and protecting their interests. But the conference did not decide all of today's borders. Most came later, through treaties, exchanges of territory and wars. How could states so far from Africa believe they had rights over these lands?

Claiming a territory is not the same as administering it. A European government could color a region on a map and declare it its own. To govern it, it needed an army, officials, and the cooperation of local authorities, or their submission. In Berlin, the powers agreed to recognize each other's colonial claims. One idea became central: [[effective occupation]]. A state had to show that it really held power over the territory it claimed.

blocks.caption: Africa around 1913, colored by colonial power: French, British, German, Portuguese, Belgian, Italian and Spanish possessions.

blocks.text: These conversations took place among Europeans. African states and rulers were not admitted on an equal footing. The powers also granted each other a [[sphere of influence]], an area where one of them held particular political and economic control. Maps and agreements became the tools of the empires. But a line on paper did not mean the people living there accepted it.

On the ground, the Europeans still had to impose their authority. Some African rulers negotiated and signed treaties. Others resisted, through diplomacy or through war. The British conquest of the [[Ashanti Kingdom]], in West Africa, shows how a war redraws the political map. The Ashanti held off British attempts to rule their country for a long time. **Britain** eventually prevailed and folded their territory into its colonial system.

blocks.caption: The Anglo-Ashanti war of 1874 in the British illustrated press: the troops march on Kumasi, the kingdom's capital.

blocks.text: Similar conflicts accompanied the French advance in the region. Colonial borders often cut through old ties: a single community found itself split between several colonies, while different peoples were gathered into the same one. Yet these populations were bound together by language, trade, religion and political alliances.

Not all colonial borders are absurd: some follow a river, a lake, a mountain range or an older political boundary. Recent research shows that precolonial states and geography shaped where some borders fell, even though European governments were the ones who made them official.

sections.title: The new states inherit the maps

blocks.text: Independence did not mean everything could be redrawn. As a rule, the new states kept the borders inherited from colonial rule. This is the principle of [[uti possidetis]], a Latin phrase: a state keeps the territory it held at the moment of independence. African leaders accepted it, because redrawing the borders would have led to endless conflicts and new wars.

Many would still have liked to decide which community belonged to which state, and which historical boundaries should prevail. The [[Organization of African Unity]] (OAU), founded in **1963**, nevertheless accepted the existing territorial order. A year later, its leaders pledged to respect the borders each state held at the moment of independence.

blocks.caption: African heads of state gathered in Addis Ababa in May 1963 for the founding conference of the Organization of African Unity.

blocks.text: The OAU's decision did not rest on the belief that these borders were fair. Its leaders feared that reopening every territorial question after independence would drag the continent into widespread conflict.

So who drew Africa's borders? European governments shaped most of the framework, through conquest, treaties, colonial rule and diplomatic bargaining. But today's lines also reflect the resistance of African societies, the negotiations with local rulers and the decisions taken after independence. The straight lines do exist, but the Europeans did not simply draw them with a ruler.

events.title: Inherited borders

blocks.text: Above all, a border is not just a line on a map. It decides which state you belong to, which laws you live under and where you can move freely. Political choices made in colonial times still shape lives today, long after the empires that made them have disappeared.

Africa's borders have not one author but many: European empires set the framework, African societies fought or negotiated it, and the independent states chose to keep it rather than risk endless wars.
